newsitem.title: USA: Clinton insists on limited tax cuts in budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton insists on limited tax cuts in budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday he had high hopes a balanced budget agreement was within reach but insisted it must contain only "disciplined" tax cuts that would not inflate deficits again in the future.

"We have to be very careful not to set conditions in motion which could explode the deficit again because of the way the tax cut is written or other provisions are written after this budget period ends," Clinton said. He referred to negotiations with Republican congressional leaders to balance the federal budget by 2002.

Clinton commented in a statement claiming new low U.S. unemployment figures weres a tribute to his own "new economic policy," noting that the 4.9 percent jobless rate for the month of April was the lowest such rate in 24 years. He said this achievement only underscored the need to move ahead and achieve a budget deal.

"I'm very optimistic, I'm very hopeful ... but I want to make it clear that we're moving in the right direction and this budget agreement must continue that movement, not reverse it, not undermine it," he said in reading a statement on the White House South Lawn.

The budget accord being negotiated by the White House and Republican congressional leaders would provide a five-year blueprint for spending cuts across the government and a net $85 billion to $90 billion worth of tax cuts for families and investors. It is designed to bring the federal deficit to zero by the year 2002.
"Our economy is now the strongest its been in a generation," Clinton said. "This is a great tribute to the American people and to the validity of the new economic policy we brought here in 1993."
